learn.title: Purpose, mission, objectives and performance criteria

sections.heading: Why businesses exist and what objectives do
sections.body: A business has a purpose: its underlying reason for existing and the value it aims to create. Its mission gives broad direction and identity. Objectives then turn that broad direction into intended results. A business may pursue profit, growth, survival and cash flow at the same time. Profit provides a financial return; growth may increase sales or scale; survival focuses on continuing through difficult conditions; and cash flow focuses on having sufficient cash available to meet payments. The priority given to each can change with ownership, the business’s financial position, its life stage and external conditions.

sections.heading: Comparing objectives and performance terms
sections.body: Purpose answers why the organisation exists. A mission is a broad statement of its role or direction. An objective is a result it wants to achieve. A measure or KPI is the metric used to observe performance, while a target gives a desired level or deadline for that measure. For example, improving customer service is an objective; average response time is a measure; replying within two hours by September is a target. Profit, cash and shareholder value are also different: a profitable business may still face cash shortages.

sections.heading: Mission, stakeholder priorities and social objectives
sections.body: A mission should influence the objectives selected. For instance, a mission based on affordable healthy food could lead to objectives on price and sales of healthy products. Social and ethical objectives go beyond financial return, such as lowering environmental impact, treating employees and suppliers fairly, ethical sourcing or community support. They may strengthen reputation and customer loyalty, but can increase costs or constrain short-run profit. Mission emphasis is shaped by ownership, founder values, stakeholder expectations, life stage, financial position and external forces such as competition, technology, law and social attitudes. These links connect strategy with stakeholder management and operational decisions.

sections.heading: A mission influence in context
sections.body: Example: After a new owner buys a clothing retailer, they place greater value on ethical sourcing. The mission may gradually place more emphasis on responsible supply chains, followed by objectives for supplier standards. A financial crisis could instead make survival and cash generation more prominent. Non-example: calling a KPI dashboard a mission. A dashboard contains measures; it does not explain the business’s broad purpose or intended role.

sections.heading: Do not confuse a KPI with the objective
sections.body: A KPI is not an objective. The objective is the result sought; the KPI is evidence used to judge progress. Likewise, a SMART objective is not automatically strategically good. It may be specific and timed but still conflict with the mission or create harmful incentives. If a call centre targets shorter calls alone, employees may rush customers and reduce first-contact resolution. The target is met, but the underlying customer objective is weakened.

sections.heading: Check alignment and trade-offs
sections.body: Choose a local business and explain: (1) why it exists; (2) one likely financial objective and one non-financial or ethical objective; (3) how its ownership or financial position might influence its mission; and (4) one target that could cause unintended behaviour. Then state an additional measure that would reduce the risk of staff simply gaming the target.

key_terms.definition: The underlying reason an organisation exists.
A broad statement of a business’s direction or intended role.
A result that a business seeks to achieve.
A metric used to observe performance.
A desired level or deadline attached to a measure.
An aim to generate a financial surplus or return.
An aim to increase the scale of the business, such as sales or output.
An aim to continue operating, especially during difficult conditions.
An aim to maintain enough cash to meet payments when due.
Goals beyond financial return, such as reducing environmental impact or treating stakeholders fairly.

items.prompt: What is meant by the purpose of a business?
items.answer: Its underlying reason for existing and the value it intends to create.
items.explanation: Purpose is broader than a specific objective or a performance measure.

items.prompt: A café wants enough money in its bank account to pay wages and rent on time. Which objective is most directly relevant: profit, growth, survival or cash flow?
items.explanation: The issue is the availability of cash to make payments, rather than the level of accounting profit or the scale of sales.

items.prompt: Compare a survival objective with a growth objective for a small retailer facing a sharp fall in demand.
items.answer: Survival prioritises continuing to trade and preserving cash, whereas growth aims to increase the scale of the business. In a sharp downturn, survival is likely to be the more immediate priority because expansion could use scarce cash and increase risk.
items.explanation: Objectives can change in importance when financial conditions change.

items.prompt: A Manchester cosmetics business changes to recyclable packaging, increasing its costs. Identify one social or ethical objective this could support and one possible short-run drawback.
items.answer: It could support reducing environmental impact. A short-run drawback is higher costs, which may reduce profit or require higher prices.
items.explanation: Ethical objectives can support reputation and loyalty but may involve financial trade-offs.

items.prompt: A shareholder-owned delivery firm is acquired by a social enterprise after repeated customer complaints about worker treatment. Judge whether its mission is likely to change quickly or gradually.
items.answer: It is likely to be rewritten or substantially changed because a change of owner and strong stakeholder concerns can alter the values shaping mission. However, changes in actual operations may take longer to implement.
items.explanation: Mission emphasis usually develops gradually, but a new owner or crisis can trigger a rewrite.

items.prompt: A student says, “Our KPI is customer satisfaction, so customer satisfaction is our objective.” Is this accurate?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Customer satisfaction can be the objective, but the KPI is the measure used to observe it, such as a survey score or complaint rate.
items.explanation: An objective is the intended result; a KPI is a metric. They should not be treated as the same thing.

items.prompt: A food delivery business has a mission to provide affordable, reliable meals. It sets a target to cut delivery time but riders begin taking unsafe shortcuts and customer complaints rise. Select the best recommendation: A) keep only the delivery-time target because it is measurable; B) remove all targets; C) use delivery time alongside safety and customer-outcome measures, and review the target; D) focus only on profit.
items.answer: C) Use delivery time alongside safety and customer-outcome measures, and review the target.
items.explanation: A single target can distort behaviour. A balanced set of measures better reflects the mission and reduces harmful local optimisation.
